svg.title: EVPN's core idea: a MAC address becomes a BGP route, and five design consequences that follow from it
svg.desc: Left panel: in the VPLS world a MAC is learned in the data plane, drawn as a MAC table filled by flooding with an ageing timer beside it, so state is built by traffic and lost when the timer expires. Right panel: in the EVPN world the same MAC is a BGP route card carrying a next hop, an ESI, a mobility sequence number and communities. Below, five consequences follow as direct deductions: MAC movement becomes a route update, flood based learning disappears, route attributes enable traffic engineering and aliasing, BGP multihoming gives all active links without MC-LAG, and a control plane that knows the MACs can answer ARP on their behalf.
svg.text: Change one assumption and every EVPN advantage becomes a deduction, not a feature list
A MAC is not a fact about the wire — in EVPN it is a route with a next hop, attributes and policy
a MAC is learned from traffic
entries appear only after traffic arrives
State is built by traffic, aged out by a timer, and rebuilt by flooding.
nothing in the network knows a MAC before it speaks
encap MPLS or VXLAN · route type carries intent
a withdraw is as fast as a route update
State is carried by the control plane, so it can be reasoned about,
filtered by policy and withdrawn in one message.
VM migration is a route update: convergence in seconds, and no duplicate-MAC alarm
Flood-based learning disappears; recovery becomes a BGP withdraw, not a re-flood
Traffic engineering and aliasing: several PEs can share the load for one CE
All-Active multihoming is native — no MC-LAG, no cross-device coordination
The control plane knows the MACs
ARP proxying becomes possible, so BUM traffic drops even before you tune anything
Every row above is a corollary, not a feature. The exam question is rarely "what does EVPN do"; it is "which of these follow from the assumption, and which need extra design work".
